intuition: Enumerating subsets of candidate indices finds target sums but creates duplicate value combinations whenever the input repeats a number. Deduplicating only afterward spends time on branches known to be equivalent. Sorting lets us recognize that equivalence before exploring the branch.

At one recursion depth, choosing a later copy of the same value creates the same family of continuations as choosing the first available copy. Skip those equal sibling choices. However, another copy remains valid at a deeper depth: [1,1,6] uses two different indices and must not be removed by a global duplicate rule.

The recursion carries the next usable index and remaining sum. Moving to i+1 prevents an index from being reused. Positive sorted values also permit early stopping once a candidate exceeds the remaining budget, because every later candidate is at least as large. Save a copy when the budget becomes exactly zero.

steps: Sort the first fixture into [1,1,2,5,6,7,10], with target 8 and an empty path.
Choose the first 1, then the second 1. Their remaining budget is 6; trying value 6 eventually produces [1,1,6].
Backtrack to path [1]. Choosing 2 leaves budget 5, so choosing 5 produces [1,2,5].
From path [1], choosing 7 also completes the budget and records [1,7]. Other over-budget continuations stop at their first too-large value.
At the root, skip the second 1 because it is an equal sibling choice. Choosing 2 then 6 produces [2,6].
No later root choice can form another sum. Return these four combinations, each recorded once despite the duplicated input 1.

codeNotes.note: Skip equal alternatives only among siblings of the same call. An equal value at start can still be used in a deeper combination.
Advancing past the chosen index enforces one use per input occurrence while carrying the unfinished target to the next call.
Backtracking mutates path after a result is found. A copy freezes the completed combination instead of letting later removals erase it.
